question: How does Hilt work internally? How does it create dependencies and manage their lifecycle?
intro: Hilt is a dependency injection library built on top of Dagger that generates the code required to create and provide dependencies automatically.

sections.title: How does Hilt work?
points: @HiltAndroidApp initialises the application's dependency injection setup.
@Inject tells Hilt which constructor or field needs dependency injection.
@Module, @Provides, and @Binds define how dependencies are provided.
Hilt generates the dependency graph at compile time.

sections.title: How are objects created?
sections.text: When a class requests a dependency, Hilt follows the generated dependency graph, creates the required objects, and supplies them automatically.

sections.title: How does Hilt manage lifecycle?
sections.text: Hilt uses components and scopes to control how long dependency instances are retained.
points: @Singleton: one instance per SingletonComponent instance, typically the application.
@ViewModelScoped: one instance within a given ViewModel component.

keyPoint: Hilt generates dependency injection code at compile time, while component scopes determine instance reuse and lifetime.

question: What are Extension Functions in Kotlin? How do they work internally, and how are they different from inheritance?

sections.title: What are Extension Functions?
sections.text: Extension functions let us add a new function to an existing class without modifying its code or creating a subclass.

sections.title: How do they work internally?
sections.text: Kotlin does not actually add the function to the original class. On the JVM, the compiler turns a top-level extension function into a static method that takes the object as a parameter.

sections.title: Extension Functions vs Inheritance
points: Extension functions: add convenience functions without changing the class or its hierarchy.
Inheritance: creates a parent-child relationship, allowing a subclass to reuse and, where permitted, override parent behaviour.

keyPoint: Extensions add functionality from the outside; inheritance extends a class through a parent-child relationship.

question: Q. When would you use a Foreground Service instead of WorkManager?
intro:
Answer:
It depends on whether the task needs to run as an ongoing, user-visible operation or can be deferred.

sections.title: ✅ Foreground Service  Keeps an ongoing task active and visible to the user. Shows a persistent notification. Example: Playing music while the user navigates to another app.  ✅ WorkManager  Schedules work that should execute reliably when system conditions allow. Supports network constraints, retries, and persistent work. Example: Uploading pending data when an internet connection becomes available.

keyPoint: 📌 Interview Tip: WorkManager does not guarantee immediate execution. A Foreground Service is not a replacement for all background work either; it must satisfy Android's foreground-service restrictions.
